p: One theory holds that the shadoof was invented in Mesopotamia as early as the time of Sargon of Akkad, around the 24th and 23rd centuries BCE. The Minoans are believed to have adopted it next, with evidence of its use from around 2100–1600 BCE. Its appearance in Upper Egypt is placed most likely in the 18th Dynasty. Some historians believe instead that the Egyptians invented it along the Nile, citing tomb drawings of shadoofs at Thebes from 1250 BCE. A third theory places its origin in India at about the same time as in Mesopotamia, because it was so widespread there, but little other evidence supports it.

The pole is hung on its frame about one-fifth of its length from one end. The vessel on the long arm may be a bucket, a skin bag or a reed basket coated with bitumen, and some have an uneven base or a tie at the top so that the water runs out at once. The operator pushes the vessel down with his own weight, and the counterweight raises it full without effort. The water is emptied into runnels that carry it along irrigation ditches. The frame may be one post or a pair, and the vessel may hang from a rope or from a thinner stick.

The device lifts water from 1 to 6 metres, and its efficiency has been calculated at 60 per cent. A study in Nigeria, which measured effort by heart rate, found that suitable adjustments reduced the energy the operator spent from about 109 to 71 watts.

In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia shadoofs set in tiers, one above another, raised water to higher levels by the work of several people. In Egypt under the Middle and New Kingdoms, pleasure gardens watered by shadoof became a mark of luxury residences and a symbol of status. Women have often worked it, since it is easy to use.

The name comes from the Arabic šādūf; in English it is also called a well sweep or swape. The ancient Greeks knew it as the kēlōn or kēlōneion, the Chinese call it jiégāo, and its Hungarian name, gémeskút, means heron well. Today it is very common in rural India and Pakistan, and in Europe in Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and Germany. On the Great Hungarian Plain it is considered a symbol of the region.

notes: The article writes 'sometime after 2000 BC, most likely during the 18th Dynasty', which do not sit well together (the 18th Dynasty is much later than 2000 BCE); the existing description already has 'after 2000 BCE', so I gave only the dynasty, attributed as 'is placed'.
The Chad figures (39-130 litres a minute) are already in the description and not repeated.
The article's Social effects section is essay-like and unsourced; I took only its concrete statements (tiered shadoofs, Egyptian pleasure gardens, women operating it).
'operator ... his own weight': the article says 'their own weight'; change if preferred.
